proof: Write f(z)=f(a)+(z−a)g(z); the constant term integrates to 2πi f(a) and the remaining term has a holomorphic integrand, so its integral vanishes by Cauchy's theorem.
consequence: It yields the mean value property, derivative estimates and the analyticity of holomorphic functions.

title: The Residue Theorem
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: The integral of a meromorphic function around a closed contour equals 2πi times the sum of residues at singularities inside the contour.
short: Contour integrals count the residues hidden inside the loop.
detail: The residue is the coefficient of (z−a)^{-1} in the Laurent expansion.
proof: Subtract the principal parts at the finitely many interior singularities; the remainder is holomorphic, so Cauchy's theorem gives zero, while each principal part contributes 2πi times its residue.
consequence: It evaluates many real integrals and sums that are inaccessible by elementary methods.

title: The Argument Principle
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: For a meromorphic function f on a contour, the change in argument of f along the contour equals 2πi times the number of zeros minus the number of poles inside, counted with multiplicity.
short: Winding of f around zero counts zeros and poles.
detail: The logarithmic derivative has simple poles with residues equal to multiplicities at zeros and minus multiplicities at poles.
proof: Apply the residue theorem to f'/f; near a zero of order m the logarithmic derivative has residue m, and near a pole of order n it has residue −n.
consequence: It powers numerical root finding and Rouché's theorem.

title: Rouché's Theorem for Counting Zeros
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: If f and g are holomorphic inside and on a contour and |g| < |f| on the contour, then f and f+g have the same number of zeros inside the contour.
short: A dominant function determines the zero count even after a small perturbation.
detail: It is proved by homotoping f to f+g and applying the argument principle.
proof: The family f+tg never vanishes on the contour, so the argument-principle count is constant in t by continuity.
consequence: It locates roots of polynomials and proves results such as the fundamental theorem of algebraically closed fields.

title: The Maximum Modulus Principle
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: A nonconstant holomorphic function on a domain cannot attain its maximum modulus at an interior point.
latex: |f| \text{ has no interior maximum unless } f \text{ constant}
short: Holomorphic functions push their largest values out to the boundary.
detail: For a bounded domain the supremum of |f| occurs on the boundary if f extends continuously.
proof: If an interior maximum existed, the mean value property over small circles would force f to be constant on each circle and hence on a neighbourhood, then throughout the domain.
consequence: It gives the fundamental theorem of algebra and bounds in interpolation theory.

title: The Minimum Modulus Principle
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: A nonconstant holomorphic function on a domain that never vanishes cannot attain a positive minimum modulus in the interior.
latex: f\ne0 \text{ and nonconstant} \Rightarrow |f| \text{ has no interior minimum}
short: Apply the maximum principle to the reciprocal of a nonvanishing function.
detail: If zeros are allowed, the minimum is zero and is attained at those zeros.
proof: Since 1/f is holomorphic when f has no zeros, an interior minimum of |f| would be an interior maximum of |1/f|, contradicting the maximum modulus principle.
consequence: It is used in factorisation theory and in proving that injective holomorphic maps have nonvanishing derivative.

title: Liouville's Theorem for Bounded Entire Functions
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: Every bounded entire function is constant.
latex: f \text{ entire and bounded} \Rightarrow f \text{ constant}
short: A globally bounded holomorphic function has no room to vary.
detail: The result is special to the complex setting; bounded entire real-variable analogues do not exist.
proof: Cauchy's estimate gives |f'(a)| ≤ M/R for every radius R; letting R tend to infinity forces f' to vanish everywhere.
consequence: It gives a short proof of the fundamental theorem of algebra and characterises entire functions of polynomial growth.

title: The Casorati–Weierstrass Theorem
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: Near an essential singularity, a holomorphic function comes arbitrarily close to every complex value.
short: Essential singularities scramble every neighbourhood across the whole complex plane.
detail: Picard's great theorem strengthens this to attaining every value except possibly one infinitely often.
proof: If some value were avoided in a punctured neighbourhood, then 1/(f−w) would be bounded near the singularity; the removable singularity theorem and Liouville-type arguments would force a pole or removable point, contradicting essentialness.
consequence: It illustrates the extreme behaviour of essential singularities.

title: Picard's Little Theorem
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: A nonconstant entire function omits at most one complex value.
short: An entire function cannot miss two different complex numbers.
detail: The exponential function misses exactly zero, so the bound is sharp.
proof: If an entire function omitted two values, composing with a suitable Möbius map and an elliptic modular function would produce a bounded entire function, which Liouville's theorem forces to be constant.
consequence: It is a striking demonstration of the rigidity of entire functions.

title: Laurent Series in Annular Domains
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: A function holomorphic in an annulus expands uniquely as a doubly infinite series in powers of z−a, converging throughout the annulus.
short: Around a singularity, a function may need negative powers as well as positive ones.
detail: The coefficients are contour integrals around a circle in the annulus.
proof: Apply Cauchy's integral formula on the boundary of a truncated annulus and subtract the two circular integrals; the difference gives the full Laurent expansion.
consequence: Laurent series classify singularities and define residues.

title: Classification of Isolated Singularities by Laurent Series
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: An isolated singularity is removable exactly when the principal part of the Laurent series vanishes, a pole of order m when the lowest power is −m, and essential when infinitely many negative powers occur.
short: The negative-power tail of a Laurent series tells you what kind of singularity you have.
detail: Removable singularities can be filled in by defining the missing value as the limit.
proof: If the principal part is finite with lowest exponent −m, multiplying by (z−a)^m removes the singularity and yields a pole; if it is infinite, the singularity is neither removable nor a pole, hence essential.
consequence: It gives a mechanical test for singularity type and is the first step in residue calculus.

title: Meromorphic Functions and Poles of Finite Order
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: A function is meromorphic on a domain if it is holomorphic except at isolated points that are poles, where it tends to infinity like a negative power.
latex: f(z)\sim c(z-a)^{-m} \text{ near a pole of order } m
short: Meromorphic functions are holomorphic functions allowed to have controlled infinities.
detail: They form a field under pointwise addition and multiplication.
proof: A pole of order m means (z−a)^m f(z) extends holomorphically with a nonzero value, so the local description follows from the Laurent expansion.
consequence: Meromorphic functions are the natural objects of the argument principle and of Riemann surface theory.

title: The Riemann Mapping Theorem
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: Every nonempty simply connected proper open subset of the complex plane is conformally equivalent to the open unit disc.
short: All simply connected planar domains except the whole plane are the same conformally.
detail: The map is unique once a point and a direction are specified.
proof: Normal families and Montel's theorem give a maximiser of derivative norm among injective maps into the disc; the maximiser is shown surjective by a square-root trick and Schwarz's lemma.
consequence: It is the foundational uniformisation result for planar domains.

title: Schwarz's Lemma on Holomorphic Self-Maps of the Disc
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: If f maps the unit disc to itself holomorphically with f(0)=0, then |f(z)| ≤ |z| and |f'(0)| ≤ 1, with equality in either inequality only for a rotation f(z)=e^{iθ}z.
short: A disc-preserving map fixing the origin is a contraction unless it is a rotation.
detail: The Schwarz–Pick lemma generalises this to maps fixing an arbitrary point of the disc.
proof: Apply the maximum modulus principle to f(z)/z on shrinking discs and let the radius tend to one; equality forces the quotient to be constant of modulus one.
consequence: It is a key tool in geometric function theory and in the proof of the Riemann mapping theorem.

title: The Schwarz–Christoffel Mapping
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: A conformal map from the upper half-plane to the interior of a polygon has derivative given by a product of powers (z−x_k)^{α_k−1} where the x_k are prevertices and α_k π are the interior angles.
short: Polygon angles translate into exponents in the derivative of the conformal map.
detail: The prevertices are determined by the side lengths and must usually be found numerically.
proof: The argument of each factor is constant along a segment of the real axis, so the image of each interval is a straight line; the exponent determines the turning angle at each prevertex.
consequence: It gives explicit conformal maps for polygonal domains used in fluid flow and electrostatics.

title: Möbius Transformations as Automorphisms of the Riemann Sphere
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: The maps z↦(az+b)/(cz+d) with ad−bc nonzero are exactly the conformal automorphisms of the Riemann sphere and act sharply three-transitively on the sphere.
short: Fractional linear maps are the rigid motions of complex projective geometry.
detail: They map generalised circles to generalised circles and preserve cross-ratios.
proof: Matrices in GL(2,C) give the maps, scalar matrices give the same map, and a Möbius transformation is determined by the images of three distinct points.
consequence: They are the basic coordinate changes in complex analysis and hyperbolic geometry.

title: Conformality of Holomorphic Maps with Nonzero Derivative
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: A holomorphic function with nonzero derivative at a point preserves angles and orientation there.
short: Multiplication by a complex number is a rotation and a scaling, so angles survive.
detail: The conformal factor is |f'(a)|, so infinitesimal shapes are scaled uniformly in all directions.
proof: The derivative acts as multiplication by the complex number f'(a), whose real linear matrix is a scalar times a rotation, and such matrices preserve angles.
consequence: It explains why holomorphic maps give isothermal coordinates and preserve the shapes of infinitesimal figures.

title: Harmonic Functions and the Mean Value Property
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: The real and imaginary parts of a holomorphic function are harmonic and satisfy the mean value property: the value at the centre equals the average over any small circle.
short: Harmonic functions are exactly those whose value is the average of their neighbours.
detail: Conversely every harmonic function on a simply connected domain has a harmonic conjugate.
proof: The mean value property follows from the real part of Cauchy's formula; applying the Laplacian in polar coordinates to the averaging identity gives Δu=0.
consequence: It links complex analysis to potential theory and the physical theory of steady-state heat flow.

title: The Poisson Kernel and the Dirichlet Problem on the Disc
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: For continuous boundary data g on the unit circle, the Poisson integral solves the Dirichlet problem for the Laplace equation on the open unit disc.
short: The Poisson kernel averages boundary values into a harmonic interior function.
detail: The kernel is the real part of (e^{it}+z)/(e^{it}−z) and tends to a Dirac mass as r approaches one.
proof: Each Poisson kernel is harmonic in z and has boundary integral reproducing continuous data via an approximate identity argument.
consequence: It solves the classical Dirichlet problem explicitly on the disc and motivates Green's functions.

title: The Identity Theorem for Holomorphic Functions
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: Two holomorphic functions on a connected domain that agree on a set with an accumulation point in the domain agree everywhere.
latex: f=g \text{ on set with limit point in } \Omega \Rightarrow f\equiv g
short: Holomorphic functions are determined by arbitrarily small pieces of data.
detail: The accumulation point must lie inside the domain, not on its boundary.
proof: Zeros of a nonzero holomorphic function are isolated because the power series at a zero has a first nonzero coefficient; an accumulation point of agreement would force all coefficients to vanish locally and then everywhere by connectedness.
consequence: It underlies analytic continuation and the principle of uniqueness of analytic functions.

title: Hadamard's Gap Theorem and Natural Boundaries
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: If the exponents in a power series grow with bounded lacunarity, meaning n_{k+1}/n_k exceeds a fixed ratio greater than one, then the circle of convergence is a natural boundary across which no analytic continuation is possible.
short: Large gaps in a power series can seal its convergence circle completely.
detail: The series sum z^{2^k} has the unit circle as a natural boundary.
proof: Hadamard's argument exploits the functional relation implied by the exponents; singularities at roots of unity become dense on the circle and block continuation through any arc.
consequence: It shows that the disc of convergence can be a genuine obstacle, not merely a limitation of a particular expansion.

title: The Gamma Function and Its Functional Equation
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: The Gamma function extends the factorial by Γ(z)=integral of t^{z−1}e^{−t} for Re z>0 and satisfies Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z) and Γ(n+1)=n!.
short: Gamma interpolates factorials to complex arguments.
detail: It is meromorphic with simple poles at nonpositive integers and has no zeros.
proof: Integrating by parts gives the functional equation; evaluating Γ(1)=1 then gives the factorial values by induction.
consequence: It appears in analysis, number theory, statistics and the functional equation of the zeta function.

title: Euler's Formula and the Identity e^{iπ}+1=0
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: For every real angle θ, e^{iθ}=cos θ + i sin θ, so in particular e^{iπ}+1=0.
short: Exponentiation with an imaginary exponent traces the unit circle.
detail: The identity links five fundamental constants in a single equation.
proof: Compare the real and imaginary parts of the power series for exp(iθ) with those of cosine and sine, or note both solve y''=−y with the same initial data.
consequence: It underlies phasors, signal processing and the complex exponential's periodicity.

title: De Moivre's Formula and Roots of Unity
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: For integer n, (cos θ + i sin θ)^n = cos(nθ) + i sin(nθ), and the n-th roots of unity are e^{2πik/n}.
short: Raising a unit complex number to a power multiplies its angle.
detail: The roots of unity form a cyclic group under multiplication.
proof: The formula follows from Euler's formula and the law of exponents; solving z^n=1 gives the listed roots, which are distinct.
consequence: It connects trigonometry with algebra and underlies discrete Fourier analysis.

title: Jensen's Formula for Zeros inside a Disc
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: If f is holomorphic on a disc of radius R, has no zeros on the circle, and f(0) is nonzero, then the average of log|f| on the circle equals log|f(0)| plus a sum over zeros of log(R/|a|).
short: The boundary average of log magnitude records how many zeros lie inside.
detail: It is a precursor of the Jensen–Poisson formulas in value distribution theory.
proof: Factor f inside the disc using Blaschke factors for its zeros; the average of log of each Blaschke factor's boundary modulus is log(R/|a|), and the zero-free remainder contributes log|f(0)| by harmonicity.
consequence: It controls zero counting in analytic number theory and entire function theory.

title: Montel's Theorem on Normal Families
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: A family of holomorphic functions on a domain that is uniformly bounded on compact subsets is normal: every sequence has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact sets.
short: Bounded holomorphic families are precompact in the compact-open topology.
detail: The limit of such a subsequence is holomorphic by Weierstrass's theorem.
proof: Cauchy estimates give equicontinuity on compact sets; the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem then yields a locally uniformly convergent subsequence.
consequence: It is the compactness engine behind the Riemann mapping theorem and Picard's theorem.

title: The Schwarz Reflection Principle
subject: Complex Analysis
statement: A holomorphic function on a domain meeting the real axis that takes real values on the real segment extends holomorphically across that segment by f(conjugate z)=conjugate f(z).
short: Reality on a line lets you mirror a holomorphic function across it.
detail: A generalisation allows reflection across analytic arcs after a conformal change of coordinates.
proof: Define the extension by the given formula; it is continuous by the real-axis boundary condition, and Morera's theorem shows it is holomorphic because integrals over triangles cancel across the axis.
consequence: It generates analytic continuations across boundary arcs and underlies the study of Schottky groups.

title: The Division Algorithm for Integers
subject: Number Theory
statement: For integers a and b with b nonzero there exist unique integers q and r with a=qb+r and 0≤r<|b|.
short: Integer division always leaves a unique nonnegative remainder smaller than the divisor.
detail: The remainder is the residue of a modulo b.
proof: Existence follows by considering the set of values a−qb and choosing the least nonnegative one; uniqueness follows because two such remainders would differ by a multiple of b of absolute value less than |b|.
consequence: It underlies the Euclidean algorithm, modular arithmetic and unique factorisation.

title: The Euclidean Algorithm for the Greatest Common Divisor
subject: Number Theory
statement: Repeatedly replacing (a,b) by (b, a mod b) terminates at gcd(a,b) in a number of steps bounded by a constant times the number of digits of the smaller input.
short: Taking remainders repeatedly finds the gcd faster than factoring.
detail: Lamé's theorem bounds the steps by five times the number of decimal digits.
proof: The gcd is unchanged at each step, and the decreasing sequence of remainders must terminate; the last nonzero remainder divides both original numbers.
consequence: It is the standard efficient method for gcd, modular inverses and continued fractions.

title: Bézout's Identity for Integers
subject: Number Theory
statement: For integers a and b there exist integers x and y with ax+by=gcd(a,b), and the gcd is the smallest positive integer of this form.
short: The gcd is an integer linear combination of the two numbers.
detail: Back-substitution in the Euclidean algorithm produces explicit coefficients.
proof: Track each remainder of the Euclidean algorithm as a linear combination of a and b; the last nonzero remainder gives the identity.
consequence: It yields modular inverses and the proof that coprime divisors of a product are coprime to each factor.

title: The Sieve of Eratosthenes
subject: Number Theory
statement: Crossing out multiples of each prime up to sqrt(N) leaves exactly the primes up to N.
short: A simple ancient sieve generates all small primes by elimination.
detail: Every composite number up to N has a prime factor at most sqrt(N), so it is crossed out.
proof: If n is composite and n=ab with a≤b, then a≤sqrt(n)≤sqrt(N) and a has a prime divisor that the sieve removes.
consequence: It is the prototype of sieve methods in analytic number theory.

title: The Euclid–Euler Theorem on Even Perfect Numbers
subject: Number Theory
statement: Every even perfect number has the form 2^{p−1}(2^p−1) where 2^p−1 is a Mersenne prime, and every such number is perfect.
short: Even perfect numbers correspond exactly to Mersenne primes.
detail: A perfect number equals the sum of its proper divisors.
proof: Euclid proved the form always gives a perfect number; Euler proved the converse using multiplicativity of the sum-of-divisors function.
consequence: The search for even perfect numbers is identical to the search for Mersenne primes.

title: The Open Problem of Odd Perfect Numbers
subject: Number Theory
statement: It is an open problem whether any odd perfect number exists; none is known and strong necessary conditions have been proved.
short: No one knows whether a perfect number can be odd.
detail: Known constraints include being larger than 10^{1500} and having at least a large number of distinct prime factors.
proof: Open. Euler showed an odd perfect number would have the form p^{4k+1}m² with p congruent to 1 modulo 4, and extensive computations and theoretical bounds have ruled out all smaller candidates.
consequence: It is one of the oldest unsolved problems in number theory.

title: Pépin's Test for Fermat Primes
subject: Number Theory
statement: For the Fermat number F_n=2^{2^n}+1, primality is equivalent to 3^{(F_n−1)/2} being congruent to −1 modulo F_n.
short: A single modular exponentiation decides whether a Fermat number is prime.
detail: It is a specialised probabilistic-looking but deterministic primality criterion for this family.
proof: Euler's criterion and the fact that 3 is a quadratic nonresidue modulo any prime Fermat number give the forward direction; the converse uses that any prime factor of F_n is congruent to 1 modulo 2^{n+2}, forcing the order argument to contradict compositeness.
consequence: It has certified the primality or compositeness of very large Fermat numbers.

title: Euler's Totient Function and Its Product Formula
subject: Number Theory
statement: The number φ(n) of integers from 1 to n coprime to n equals n times the product over distinct primes p dividing n of (1−1/p).
short: Counting coprime residues is a product over the primes dividing n.
detail: The function is multiplicative on coprime arguments and satisfies sum_{d|n} φ(d)=n.
proof: By inclusion–exclusion over the distinct prime divisors of n, the count of integers not divisible by any of them gives the product formula.
consequence: It determines the order of the multiplicative group modulo n and underlies Euler's theorem and RSA.

title: Carmichael Numbers and Fermat Pseudoprimes
subject: Number Theory
statement: A Carmichael number is a composite n such that a^{n−1} is congruent to 1 modulo n for every a coprime to n, so it passes Fermat's primality test for all such bases.
short: Fermat's little theorem cannot be reversed: some composites fool it completely.
detail: The smallest example is 561=3·11·17, and infinitely many Carmichael numbers exist.
proof: Korselt's criterion says n is Carmichael iff it is squarefree and p−1 divides n−1 for every prime p dividing n; 561 satisfies this, and Alford–Granville–Pomerance proved infinitude.
consequence: It motivates stronger primality tests such as Miller–Rabin.

title: Primitive Roots Modulo an Odd Prime
subject: Number Theory
statement: For every prime p the multiplicative group modulo p is cyclic, so there exists a primitive root g whose powers run through all nonzero residues modulo p.
short: Modulo a prime, multiplication is generated by a single element.
detail: There are exactly φ(p−1) primitive roots modulo p.
proof: The group has order p−1; counting solutions of x^d=1 for each divisor d and using that a polynomial of degree d has at most d roots shows there is an element of exact order p−1.
consequence: It underlies discrete logarithms, primality testing and the structure of finite fields.

title: The Discrete Logarithm Problem in Number Theory
subject: Number Theory
statement: Given a prime p, a generator g of the multiplicative group modulo p and an element h, the discrete logarithm problem asks for an integer x with g^x congruent to h modulo p.
short: Finding exponents modulo a prime is believed to be hard even though exponentiation is easy.
detail: The problem is defined in any finite cyclic group, including elliptic curve groups.
proof: Exponentiation is efficiently computable by repeated squaring, while known classical algorithms for inversion, such as baby-step giant-step, require roughly sqrt of the group order operations.
consequence: Its presumed hardness underlies Diffie–Hellman key exchange and ElGamal encryption.

title: Euler's Criterion and Quadratic Residuosity
subject: Number Theory
statement: For an odd prime p and integer a not divisible by p, a is a quadratic residue modulo p if and only if a^{(p−1)/2} is congruent to 1 modulo p, and a nonresidue if and only if it is congruent to −1.
short: Exponentiation decides whether a number is a square modulo a prime.
detail: This is the computational bridge between Legendre symbols and modular powers.
proof: Euler's criterion follows because a^{(p−1)/2} squared is 1 by Fermat, and the residues are exactly the elements of the subgroup of squares of order (p−1)/2.
consequence: It is used in primality tests and in proving quadratic reciprocity.

title: Gauss's Lemma for Legendre Symbols
subject: Number Theory
statement: For an odd prime p and a not divisible by p, the Legendre symbol (a/p) equals (−1)^m where m counts the residues ka modulo p, for k=1 to (p−1)/2, that exceed p/2.
short: Counting negative representatives determines whether a is a square modulo p.
detail: It provides an elementary route to quadratic reciprocity.
proof: The least absolute residues of a,2a,...,((p−1)/2)a are distinct up to sign; their product compared with ((p−1)/2)! gives the parity count.
consequence: It is a standard first proof of quadratic reciprocity and of supplementary laws for −1 and 2.

title: The Sum of Two Squares Theorem
subject: Number Theory
statement: A positive integer n is a sum of two integer squares if and only if every prime congruent to 3 modulo 4 occurs to an even power in its factorisation.
short: Primes 3 mod 4 must appear in pairs for a representation as two squares.
detail: The representation is unique up to order and signs when n is a prime congruent to 1 modulo 4.
proof: Fermat's theorem gives a representation for such primes using minimality in a pigeonhole argument; the identity (a²+b²)(c²+d²)=(ac−bd)²+(ad+bc)² combines representations, and primes 3 mod 4 dividing x²+y² must divide both x and y.
consequence: It is a model for the arithmetic of Gaussian integers and sums-of-squares problems.

title: Lagrange's Four-Square Theorem
subject: Number Theory
statement: Every nonnegative integer is a sum of four integer squares.
short: Four squares always suffice to represent an integer.
detail: Three squares do not always suffice, for example n=7, and Legendre's three-square theorem characterises when they do.
proof: Euler's four-square identity makes the set of representable numbers closed under multiplication; it suffices to prove that every prime is representable, using a minimal-residue argument modulo p and descent.
consequence: It is the archetype of Waring-type representation theorems.

title: The Jacobi Symbol and Its Properties
subject: Number Theory
statement: The Jacobi symbol extends the Legendre symbol to odd composite moduli by multiplying Legendre symbols over the prime factors, and it satisfies quadratic reciprocity and multiplicativity.
short: Jacobi symbols let reciprocity be used without factoring the modulus.
detail: Unlike Legendre symbols, a Jacobi symbol of 1 does not guarantee that a is a square.
proof: Define the symbol from the prime factorisation and verify multiplicativity and reciprocity by reducing to the prime case, where quadratic reciprocity applies.
consequence: It enables efficient algorithms for computing Legendre symbols and is used in Solovay–Strassen primality testing.

title: Hensel's Lemma for Lifting Solutions
subject: Number Theory
statement: If an integer r satisfies f(r) congruent to 0 modulo p and f'(r) is not congruent to 0 modulo p, then r lifts uniquely to a root of f in the p-adic integers.
short: A simple root modulo p lifts to an exact root in p-adic arithmetic.
detail: The multivariate form underlies the implicit function theorem over p-adic fields.
proof: Newton-style induction constructs r_{k+1}=r_k+t p^k choosing t so that f(r_{k+1}) is divisible by p^{k+1}; the derivative condition makes t unique modulo p.
consequence: It is fundamental to p-adic analysis, local solvability and algorithmic factorisation of polynomials.

title: p-adic Numbers and the p-adic Metric
subject: Number Theory
statement: The p-adic absolute value of a nonzero rational is p to the power minus the exponent of p in its factorisation, and the p-adic numbers are the completion of the rationals in the induced metric.
short: In p-adic distance, numbers are close when their difference is highly divisible by p.
detail: The p-adic metric is ultrametric, so every triangle is isosceles with the two longer sides equal.
proof: The p-adic absolute value is multiplicative and satisfies the strong triangle inequality because v_p(x+y) is at least the minimum of the valuations; completion then gives Q_p.
consequence: p-adic fields provide the local perspective in number theory and are indispensable in modern arithmetic geometry.

title: Ostrowski's Theorem on Absolute Values of the Rationals
subject: Number Theory
statement: Every nontrivial absolute value on the rationals is equivalent either to the usual absolute value or to a p-adic absolute value for some prime p.
short: The real absolute value and the p-adic ones exhaust all possibilities on Q.
detail: This is the beginning of the local–global philosophy in number theory.
proof: If the absolute value is archimedean, raising it to a suitable power recovers the usual one; if non-archimedean, the set of integers with absolute value at most one forms an ideal generated by a prime p, giving an equivalent p-adic absolute value.
consequence: It justifies studying rational problems one prime at a time together with the real place.

title: The Hasse–Minkowski Local–Global Theorem for Quadratic Forms
subject: Number Theory
statement: A quadratic form over the rationals represents zero nontrivially if and only if it does so over the reals and over every p-adic field.
latex: q \text{ isotropic over }\mathbb{Q} \iff q \text{ isotropic over } \mathbb{R}\text{ and all }\mathbb{Q}_p
short: For quadratic forms, local solvability everywhere implies global solvability.
detail: The analogous statement fails for higher-degree forms, as the Selmer group examples show.
proof: Use the Hasse invariant and Hilbert symbols to show the local invariants determine the rational equivalence class of a quadratic form.
consequence: It is the prototype of local–global principles in arithmetic.

title: Fermat's Last Theorem
subject: Number Theory
statement: For any integer n greater than two there are no positive integers x, y, z satisfying x^n+y^n=z^n.
short: No nontrivial integer solutions exist beyond exponent two.
detail: The case n=4 was proved by Fermat by descent, and the general case remained open for over three centuries.
proof: Wiles proved the modularity theorem for semistable elliptic curves and used a hypothetical Fermat solution to build a nonmodular elliptic curve via Frey's construction, contradicting modularity.
consequence: Its proof revolutionised arithmetic geometry through modular forms and Galois representations.

title: Mihăilescu's Theorem on Consecutive Perfect Powers
subject: Number Theory
statement: The only pair of consecutive perfect powers greater than one is 8 and 9: the equation x^a−y^b=1 with x,y,a,b>1 has the unique solution 3²−2³=1.
short: Catalan's conjecture is now a theorem: 8 and 9 are the only consecutive powers.
detail: Catalan posed the conjecture in 1844; Mihăilescu proved it in 2002 using cyclotomic fields.
proof: Mihăilescu analysed cyclotomic invariants and the structure of ideal class groups in cyclotomic extensions to rule out all other exponent pairs.
consequence: It closes a classical Diophantine problem and demonstrates the power of algebraic number theory.

title: The Twin Prime Conjecture
subject: Number Theory
statement: It is an open problem whether there are infinitely many primes p such that p+2 is also prime.
short: No one knows whether pairs of primes differing by two go on forever.
detail: Zhang proved in 2013 that some even bound occurs infinitely often, later reduced to 246, and Maynard showed bounded gaps for arbitrarily many primes.
proof: Open. Hardy and Littlewood conjectured an asymptotic formula via their prime k-tuples conjecture, but no proof of infinitude of twin primes is known.
consequence: It is a central test case for sieve methods and the prime k-tuples conjecture.

title: The Goldbach Conjecture
subject: Number Theory
statement: It is an open problem whether every even integer greater than two is the sum of two primes; the analogous odd version asks for a sum of three primes.
short: Every even number appears to be a sum of two primes, but nobody can prove it.
detail: Helfgott proved the weak, odd Goldbach conjecture for all sufficiently large odd integers, building on Vinogradov's three-primes theorem.
proof: Open. Computer verification extends to very large bounds, and circle-method asymptotics are known under strong hypotheses such as the generalized Riemann hypothesis, but no unconditional proof exists.
consequence: It is one of the oldest unsolved problems in additive number theory.

title: The Riemann Hypothesis
subject: Number Theory
statement: It is an open problem whether every nontrivial zero of the Riemann zeta function has real part one half.
short: The location of zeta zeros controls the error term in the prime number theorem.
detail: The hypothesis implies strong error bounds for the prime counting function and many other arithmetic estimates.
proof: Open. The zeta function has a functional equation forcing symmetry of zeros about the critical line, and billions of zeros have been verified computationally, but a proof or disproof is unknown.
consequence: It is one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems and a cornerstone of analytic number theory.

title: Dirichlet's Approximation Theorem for Real Numbers
subject: Number Theory
statement: For any real number α and positive integer N there exist integers p and q with 1≤q≤N such that |qα−p| is at most 1/(N+1).
short: Pigeonhole guarantees surprisingly good rational approximations to any real number.
detail: It is the starting point for continued fractions and Diophantine approximation.
proof: Divide the unit interval into N+1 equal subintervals and consider the fractional parts of 0, α, 2α, ..., Nα; two lie in the same subinterval and their difference gives the required q and p.
consequence: It proves that badly approximable numbers are rare and underlies the theory of continued fractions.

title: Continued Fractions and Best Rational Approximations
subject: Number Theory
statement: The convergents of the simple continued fraction of a real number give best rational approximations: if p/q is a convergent, no rational with smaller denominator is closer to the number.
short: Truncating a continued fraction gives the best possible fraction of a given size.
detail: Convergents satisfy |α−p_n/q_n| < 1/q_n q_{n+1}.
proof: The convergents arise from the Euclidean algorithm; the recurrence p_n=a_n p_{n−1}+p_{n−2} and the alternating error identity show they approximate from alternate sides with decreasing error.
consequence: Continued fractions give efficient approximations and solve Pell's equation.

title: Lagrange's Theorem on Quadratic Continued Fractions
subject: Number Theory
statement: The simple continued fraction expansion of a quadratic irrational is eventually periodic, and conversely every eventually periodic continued fraction represents a quadratic irrational.
short: Quadratic irrationals are exactly the numbers with repeating continued fractions.
detail: For sqrt(d) the continued fraction is periodic from the first term onward, with period length related to the fundamental solution of Pell's equation.
proof: Applying the continued fraction algorithm to a quadratic irrational produces complete quotients that are reduced quadratic irrationals; only finitely many occur, so the sequence of partial quotients repeats.
consequence: It gives an algorithm for solving Pell's equation and underlies the structure of real quadratic fields.

title: Pell's Equation and Its Infinite Solutions
subject: Number Theory
statement: For a nonsquare positive integer d, the equation x²−dy²=1 has infinitely many integer solutions generated by powers of the fundamental solution.
short: A single minimal solution generates all solutions of Pell's equation.
detail: The fundamental solution can be found from the continued fraction of sqrt(d).
proof: Solutions correspond to units of norm one in the ring Z[sqrt d]; Dirichlet's unit theorem gives a fundamental unit and all totally positive powers yield solutions.
consequence: It is a classical example of the interplay between continued fractions and algebraic number theory.

title: Dirichlet Convolution and Multiplicative Functions
subject: Number Theory
statement: The Dirichlet convolution of arithmetic functions f and g is (f*g)(n)=sum over divisors d of n of f(d)g(n/d), giving a group structure on functions with f(1) nonzero.
short: Divisor sums become a convolution product with an identity element.
detail: The Möbius function is the convolution inverse of the constant-one function.
proof: Associativity follows by rearranging triple divisor sums; the identity is the function that is 1 at n=1 and 0 otherwise, and inversion is given by Möbius inversion.
consequence: It organises the relationships among divisor sums, the totient function and Dirichlet series.

title: The Dirichlet Series of the Riemann Zeta Function
subject: Number Theory
statement: For complex s with real part greater than one, the zeta function equals the sum over n of n^{-s} and also the Euler product over primes of (1−p^{-s})^{-1}.
short: Unique factorisation turns a sum over integers into a product over primes.
detail: The Euler product encodes unique factorisation analytically and fails for general Dirichlet series without multiplicativity.
proof: Expand each Euler factor as a geometric series and multiply; absolute convergence for Re s>1 justifies rearranging to obtain the sum over all integers.
consequence: It is the bridge between prime distribution and complex analysis.

title: Chebyshev's Estimates for the Prime Counting Function
subject: Number Theory
statement: There exist positive constants c and C such that c x/log x ≤ π(x) ≤ C x/log x for all large x.
short: Even before the prime number theorem, π(x) was known to have the right order of magnitude.
detail: Chebyshev also showed that if the limit of π(x) log x / x exists it must equal one.
proof: Use estimates on the logarithm of the binomial coefficient (2n choose n), whose prime factorisation encodes primes between n and 2n, to bound the Chebyshev theta function and hence π(x).
consequence: It was the first substantial step toward the prime number theorem.

title: Dirichlet's Class Number Formula
subject: Number Theory
statement: For a quadratic field, the residue at s=1 of its Dedekind zeta function equals a product involving the class number, regulator, number of roots of unity and discriminant.
short: An analytic residue encodes arithmetic data of a number field.
detail: For imaginary quadratic fields the regulator is one and the formula relates class numbers to values of Dirichlet L-functions at one.
proof: Analyse the Dedekind zeta function as a sum over ideal classes and use the geometry of numbers to count ideals of bounded norm in each class.
consequence: It initiated the use of analytic methods to obtain arithmetic information about class groups.

title: The Group Law on an Elliptic Curve
subject: Number Theory
statement: The points of a nonsingular cubic curve with a chosen point at infinity form an abelian group, where three collinear points sum to zero.
short: Drawing a line through two points defines addition on an elliptic curve.
detail: Over the reals the group has one or two components; over finite fields it is a finite abelian group.
proof: A line meets a cubic in three points counted with multiplicity, so the third intersection of the line through P and Q determines −(P+Q); associativity follows from the Cayley–Bacharach theorem or a direct algebraic verification.
consequence: It makes elliptic curves into algebraic groups and enables elliptic curve cryptography.

title: The Mordell–Weil Theorem
subject: Number Theory
statement: The group of rational points on an elliptic curve over a number field is finitely generated.
short: Rational points on an elliptic curve form a finitely generated abelian group.
detail: The rank r and the finite torsion subgroup are the basic arithmetic invariants of the curve.
proof: Descent maps E(K)/2E(K) into finitely many local cohomology groups, showing the quotient by twice the group is finite; combined with height functions this forces finite generation.
consequence: It reduces the study of rational points to determining a finite rank and torsion subgroup.

title: Hasse's Bound for Elliptic Curves over Finite Fields
subject: Number Theory
statement: For an elliptic curve over a finite field with q elements, the number of points N satisfies |N−(q+1)| ≤ 2 sqrt(q).
short: The point count deviates from q+1 by at most a square-root sized error.
detail: Equivalently the Frobenius eigenvalues on the first cohomology have absolute value sqrt(q).
proof: Hasse proved this by studying the endomorphism ring of the curve and the positive definite rosati involution, forcing the Frobenius trace to satisfy the stated inequality.
consequence: It quantifies randomness of elliptic curve point counts and underlies security estimates in cryptography.

title: The Nagell–Lutz Theorem on Torsion Points
subject: Number Theory
statement: For an elliptic curve in short Weierstrass form with integer coefficients, a rational torsion point has integer coordinates, and either y=0 or y² divides the discriminant.
short: Torsion points on an integral model have integral coordinates.
detail: It gives an effective algorithm for computing the rational torsion subgroup.
proof: Use the duplication formula and p-adic valuations to show that a torsion point cannot have a denominator, then apply the division polynomial and discriminant divisibility.
consequence: It makes the torsion part of the Mordell–Weil group algorithmically computable.

title: The Modularity Theorem for Elliptic Curves over the Rationals
subject: Number Theory
statement: Every elliptic curve over the rational numbers is modular: its L-function equals the L-function of a weight-two modular form of level equal to the conductor.
short: Elliptic curves over Q are secretly modular forms.
detail: The full statement was proved by Breuil, Conrad, Diamond and Taylor after Wiles handled the semistable case.
proof: The proof compares deformation spaces of Galois representations with modular forms using R=T theorems and Taylor–Wiles patching.
consequence: It implies Fermat's Last Theorem and opens the Langlands programme for higher-dimensional varieties.

title: The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture
subject: Number Theory
statement: It is an open problem whether the rank of an elliptic curve over Q equals the order of vanishing of its L-function at s=1.
short: The rank of rational points should be readable from an analytic L-function.
detail: The refined conjecture also predicts the leading coefficient in terms of the Tate–Shafarevich group, regulator and real period.
proof: Open. It is known in special cases, for example when the analytic rank is zero or one by work of Coates–Wiles, Gross–Zagier and Kolyvagin, but the general statement is unproved.
consequence: It is a Clay Millennium Prize Problem and a central goal of arithmetic geometry.

title: Waring's Problem and Hilbert's Solution
subject: Number Theory
statement: For every positive integer k there is a number g(k) such that every positive integer is a sum of at most g(k) k-th powers.
short: A fixed number of k-th powers always suffices to represent every integer.
detail: Lagrange's four-square theorem is the case k=2, and Hilbert proved existence for all k in 1909.
proof: Hilbert used a combinatorial identity expressing products of sums of powers as sums of powers, together with a finite difference argument and density estimates.
consequence: It founded the Hardy–Littlewood circle method approach to additive number theory.

title: Vinogradov's Three-Primes Theorem
subject: Number Theory
statement: Every sufficiently large odd integer is the sum of three primes.
short: The odd Goldbach conjecture holds beyond a finite range.
detail: Helfgott later made the result effective down to small odd integers.
proof: Vinogradov used the circle method with estimates for exponential sums over primes on minor arcs and a singular series calculation on major arcs.
consequence: It is the major milestone toward the Goldbach conjecture.

title: The Green–Tao Theorem on Primes in Arithmetic Progressions
subject: Number Theory
statement: The sequence of prime numbers contains arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions.
short: Primes, though sparse, contain arbitrarily long evenly spaced runs.
detail: Szemerédi's theorem on arithmetic progressions in dense sets does not apply directly because the primes have density zero.
proof: Green and Tao proved a relative Szemerédi theorem for pseudorandom majorants and verified that the von Mangoldt function satisfies the required linear forms and correlation conditions.
consequence: It is a landmark combining ergodic theory, additive combinatorics and analytic number theory.

title: The Hardy–Ramanujan Partition Asymptotic
subject: Number Theory
statement: The partition function p(n), counting unordered sums of positive integers, satisfies p(n) asymptotic to exp(pi sqrt(2n/3))/(4n sqrt(3)).
short: The number of partitions grows exponentially in the square root of n.
detail: Rademacher later gave an exact convergent series for p(n) using the circle method.
proof: The generating function is the reciprocal of the Euler product prod(1−q^k), and the circle method near the roots of unity gives the main term from the dominant singularity at q=1.
consequence: It is a founding success of the circle method and links partitions to modular forms.

title: Zermelo–Fraenkel Set Theory with the Axiom of Choice
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: ZFC is the standard axiomatic foundation of mathematics, consisting of the Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms together with the axiom of choice.
short: ZFC is the accepted rulebook for what counts as a set.
detail: Key axioms include extensionality, pairing, union, power set, replacement, infinity and regularity, with separation and replacement as axiom schemas.
proof: The axioms are taken as primitive; their consistency relative to weaker systems is studied via inner models and forcing, while Gödel's theorems preclude an absolute finitary consistency proof.
consequence: Almost all mainstream mathematics can be formalised in ZFC.

title: Equivalent Formulations of the Axiom of Choice
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: The axiom of choice is equivalent to Zorn's lemma, the well-ordering theorem, Tychonoff's theorem for compact spaces, and the statement that every surjection has a section.
short: Many apparently different principles are really the same choice axiom in disguise.
detail: The equivalence with Zorn's lemma is the version most often used in algebra.
proof: Each equivalence is proved by deriving one principle from another using the cumulative hierarchy and transfinite recursion; for example Zorn's lemma follows from choice by building a maximal chain.
consequence: The axiom is indispensable for many existence results but has counterintuitive consequences such as Banach–Tarski.

title: Zorn's Lemma for Maximal Elements
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If every chain in a nonempty partially ordered set has an upper bound, then the set has a maximal element.
short: Zorn's lemma produces maximal objects from chain-closed conditions.
detail: It is equivalent to the axiom of choice over ZF.
proof: Assume no maximal element and use choice to define a function selecting a strict upper bound for every element; transfinite recursion then builds a chain with no upper bound, a contradiction.
consequence: It proves existence of bases in vector spaces, maximal ideals and algebraic closures.

title: The Well-Ordering Theorem
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Every set can be well-ordered, meaning it admits a total order in which every nonempty subset has a least element.
short: Choice lets you line up any set, even an uncountable one, in a well-order.
detail: For the reals this well-order cannot be explicitly described in ZFC in any simple way.
proof: Zermelo's proof uses choice to pick an element from each nonempty subset and transfinite recursion to enumerate the set until exhausted.
consequence: It generalises induction to arbitrary sets and underlies cardinal comparison.

title: Cantor's Theorem on the Power Set
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: For every set A the power set of A has strictly larger cardinality than A.
short: There are always more subsets than elements.
detail: The diagonal argument gives an injection A into P(A) but no surjection.
proof: An injection sends a to {a}; if f:A→P(A) were surjective, the set {a∈A:a not in f(a)} would differ from every f(a), a contradiction.
consequence: It yields an infinite hierarchy of infinite cardinals.

title: The Continuum Hypothesis
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: The continuum hypothesis asserts that there is no cardinal strictly between the cardinality of the natural numbers and that of the reals.
short: Is there any infinity strictly between the countable and the continuum?
detail: The statement is neither provable nor refutable from ZFC assuming ZFC is consistent.
proof: Cantor posed it and believed it true; the status was settled only by Gödel and Cohen through constructibility and forcing.
consequence: It shows that familiar set-theoretic questions can be undecidable in the standard axioms.

title: The Independence of the Continuum Hypothesis
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Assuming ZFC is consistent, the continuum hypothesis can neither be proved nor disproved from ZFC.
short: The continuum hypothesis can be true in some models of set theory and false in others.
detail: Gödel showed CH holds in the constructible universe; Cohen showed models of ZFC where the continuum is larger than aleph-one.
proof: Gödel built the inner model L satisfying the generalized continuum hypothesis; Cohen invented forcing to add many reals while preserving ZFC, producing a model where the continuum exceeds aleph-one.
consequence: It inaugurated the modern study of independence phenomena in set theory.

title: Forcing and Generic Extensions of Models of Set Theory
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Forcing constructs a larger model of set theory by adjoining a generic filter on a partially ordered set of conditions, carefully chosen so that no new contradictions arise.
short: Forcing builds new universes of sets by adding carefully controlled generic objects.
detail: The forcing relation lets one decide in the ground model which statements the generic extension will satisfy.
proof: Start with a countable transitive model, choose a poset and an M-generic filter, define names for sets, and verify that the interpretation of all names gives a model satisfying ZFC.
consequence: It is the principal method for proving independence results across set theory.

title: The Constructible Universe L
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Gödel's constructible universe L is the class built by transfinitely iterating the operation of taking definable subsets, and it satisfies ZFC together with the generalized continuum hypothesis.
short: L is the smallest inner model containing all ordinals and satisfying ZFC.
detail: The statement that every set is constructible is the axiom V=L, which implies CH but is not forced by ZFC.
proof: Define L_α recursively using first-order definability over previous levels; verifying the ZFC axioms uses the condensation lemma, and GCH follows from a fine structure argument.
consequence: It provides the canonical inner model for relative consistency proofs.

title: Measurable Cardinals and Large Cardinal Axioms
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A measurable cardinal is an uncountable cardinal κ carrying a nonprincipal κ-complete ultrafilter; such cardinals cannot be proved to exist in ZFC alone.
short: Large cardinals are extra robustness assumptions far beyond ZFC.
detail: Measurable cardinals imply that L is not the whole universe and have strong consequences for projective determinacy.
proof: Scott's theorem shows that if a measurable cardinal exists then V differs from L, since the ultrapower by a measure would otherwise contradict rigidity of L.
consequence: They form a hierarchy measuring the consistency strength of strong set-theoretic statements.

title: Ordinal Arithmetic and Its Noncommutativity
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Ordinal addition, multiplication and exponentiation are defined by transfinite recursion and are generally noncommutative; for example 1+ω=ω but ω+1>ω.
short: For infinite ordinals, the order of operations matters.
detail: Ordinal arithmetic describes order types rather than sizes, unlike cardinal arithmetic.
proof: Ordinal addition is defined by concatenating well-orders, so appending one point after all naturals gives a different order type from putting it before them.
consequence: It is the algebra of transfinite processes and induction.

title: Transfinite Induction and Recursion
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If a property holds at zero, at successors whenever it holds at the predecessor, and at limit ordinals whenever it holds at all earlier ordinals, then it holds for every ordinal.
short: Induction works on ordinals provided one handles limit stages separately.
detail: Transfinite recursion similarly defines functions on all ordinals from their earlier values.
proof: If some ordinal failed the property, the least such ordinal could not be zero, a successor or a limit, a contradiction.
consequence: It underlies constructions such as the cumulative hierarchy and well-ordering proofs.

title: The Burali-Forti Paradox
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: The collection of all ordinals cannot itself be a set, since it would be well-ordered and hence an ordinal larger than every ordinal, including itself.
short: The ordinals are too numerous to form a completed set.
detail: A similar paradox arises for the collection of all cardinals.
proof: Any set of ordinals has a supremum which is an ordinal greater than all its members; applying this to the alleged set of all ordinals gives a contradiction.
consequence: It motivates the set/class distinction in axiomatic set theory.

title: Russell's Paradox and the Limits of Naive Comprehension
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: The set of all sets that are not members of themselves cannot exist, because it is a member of itself exactly when it is not.
latex: R=\{x:x\notin x\},\quad R\in R\iff R\notin R
short: Unrestricted set formation is logically inconsistent.
detail: Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory replaces comprehension by separation, allowing only subsets of an existing set.
proof: Assume R is a set; asking whether R belongs to R gives the contradiction directly from its definition.
consequence: It forced the axiomatisation of set theory and reshaped the foundations of mathematics.

title: The Schröder–Bernstein Theorem
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If there are injections from A into B and from B into A, then there is a bijection between A and B.
short: Mutual embeddability of sets forces equal cardinality.
detail: The proof does not require the axiom of choice.
proof: Track elements under alternating applications of the two injections; partition each set into chains and cycles and define a bijection by following the injections on one family of chains and their inverses on the rest.
consequence: It defines cardinal comparison without needing a well-ordering of the sets.

title: König's Theorem on Cardinal Sums
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If κ_i < λ_i for every i in an index set, then the sum of the κ_i is strictly less than the product of the λ_i.
short: A product of larger cardinals always outruns a sum of smaller ones.
detail: The special case with all κ_i finite and λ_i=2 gives Cantor's theorem.
proof: Given a map from the disjoint union into the product, diagonalise by choosing for each index a value of λ_i not used by the corresponding component.
consequence: It gives the consistency of the axiom of choice with ZF and strong inequalities in cardinal arithmetic.

title: The Hartogs Number of a Set
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: For every set A there is a least ordinal that cannot be injected into A, called the Hartogs number of A.
short: Every set has a well-ordered size that it cannot absorb.
detail: Hartogs numbers exist in ZF without the axiom of choice and give the smallest well-ordered cardinal not dominated by A.
proof: Consider the set of well-orderings of subsets of A and take the supremum of their order types; the next ordinal cannot inject into A.
consequence: It is used to prove that every set can be well-ordered if and only if the axiom of choice holds.

title: Łoś's Theorem and Ultraproducts
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: In an ultraproduct of structures, a first-order sentence holds in the ultraproduct if and only if the set of indices where it holds belongs to the ultrafilter.
short: Ultraproducts transfer first-order truth from components modulo an ultrafilter.
detail: Łoś's theorem is the fundamental theorem of ultraproducts and underlies nonstandard analysis.
proof: Prove by induction on formulas; atomic cases follow from the definition, boolean connectives use ultrafilter closure, and existential quantifiers use a choice function on a set in the ultrafilter.
consequence: It yields compactness, nonstandard models of the reals and transfer principles.

title: Quantifier Elimination in Model Theory
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A theory has quantifier elimination if every formula is equivalent modulo the theory to a formula containing no quantifiers.
short: Quantifier elimination reduces logical complexity to explicit conditions.
detail: The theory of algebraically closed fields and the theory of real closed fields both have quantifier elimination in suitable languages.
proof: Eliminate one quantifier at a time by constructing a quantifier-free equivalent using the algebraic or order-theoretic structure, then iterate.
consequence: It yields decidability and geometric descriptions of definable sets.

title: The Tarski–Vaught Test for Elementary Substructures
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A subset A of a structure M is the universe of an elementary substructure if and only if every existential formula with parameters from A that holds in M has a witness in A.
short: Elementary substructures are exactly those that realise every existential demand they can express.
detail: The test is the standard tool for building elementary chains.
proof: Induct on formula complexity; atomic and boolean cases are immediate, and the existential direction is precisely the stated witness condition.
consequence: It is used in the downward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem and in model-theoretic constructions.

title: Gödel's Completeness Theorem for First-Order Languages
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A first-order sentence is provable from a theory if and only if it is true in every model of that theory.
short: Syntactic provability and semantic truth coincide in first-order logic.
detail: This is distinct from Gödel's incompleteness theorems, which concern the limits of particular theories.
proof: Show that every consistent theory has a model by constructing a term model from maximal consistent sets (Henkin's proof), then apply contraposition.
consequence: It legitimises model-theoretic reasoning as a substitute for syntactic derivation.

title: The Compactness Theorem for First-Order Logic
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A set of first-order sentences has a model if and only if every finite subset has a model.
short: Finite consistency is enough to guarantee an infinite model.
detail: It yields nonstandard models of arithmetic and the existence of infinite models from arbitrarily large finite ones.
proof: Combine completeness with the observation that if the whole set were inconsistent, a finite subset would already be inconsistent because formal proofs are finite.
consequence: It is one of the most powerful tools in model theory.

title: The Löwenheim–Skolem Theorems
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If a first-order theory in a countable language has an infinite model, it has models of every infinite cardinality at least the size of the language.
short: First-order theories cannot control the infinite size of their models.
detail: Skolem's paradox is that set theory has countable models even though it proves uncountable sets exist.
proof: Use the downward theorem with elementary substructures generated by a chosen subset and the upward theorem by adding fresh constants and applying compactness.
consequence: It limits the expressive power of first-order logic and is central to model theory.

title: The Deduction Theorem
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: A theory proves an implication from premise to conclusion exactly when extending the theory by that premise proves the conclusion.
short: Conditional proofs correspond to proving the consequent with the antecedent assumed.
detail: It holds for standard Hilbert-style and natural deduction systems for first-order logic.
proof: The forward direction uses modus ponens; the converse transforms any proof from the extended theory into a proof of the implication by induction on proof length.
consequence: It is the formal justification for the everyday method of conditional proof.

title: The Soundness Theorem for First-Order Logic
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: If a sentence is formally provable from a theory, then it is true in every model of that theory.
short: The proof system never proves something false in all models.
detail: Soundness is the converse half of Gödel's completeness theorem.
proof: Verify that the axioms are valid in every model and that the inference rules, especially modus ponens and generalisation, preserve truth; induction on proof length completes the argument.
consequence: It guarantees that syntactic derivation is a reliable guide to semantic truth.

title: Gentzen's Consistency Proof for Peano Arithmetic
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Gentzen proved the consistency of Peano arithmetic using transfinite induction up to the ordinal epsilon-zero, a principle not available inside Peano arithmetic itself.
short: Peano arithmetic is consistent, but proving so needs stronger ordinal methods.
detail: The result illustrates Gödel's second incompleteness theorem: the consistency statement is not provable in PA itself.
proof: Gentzen assigned ordinals below epsilon-zero to sequent derivations and showed cut elimination reduces ordinals, so an inconsistency would yield an infinite descending ordinal sequence, which transfinite induction forbids.
consequence: It founded ordinal analysis and proof theory.

title: Gentzen's Cut Elimination Theorem
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: Any proof in sequent calculus can be transformed into a proof of the same sequent that does not use the cut rule.
short: Cuts can be pushed into the subproofs, yielding analytic proofs.
detail: The subformula property of cut-free proofs gives consistency and decidability consequences.
proof: Successively reduce the complexity of cut formulas and the height of derivations by permuting cuts upward until they disappear.
consequence: It is the central theorem of structural proof theory and underlies automated theorem proving.

title: The Axiom of Regularity and the Cumulative Hierarchy
subject: Set Theory & Logic
statement: The axiom of regularity says every nonempty set has an element disjoint from it, which forbids infinite descending membership chains and supports the cumulative hierarchy picture of sets.
short: Sets are built in layers, with no circular membership loops.
detail: The rank of a set is the least ordinal stage at which it appears in the hierarchy.
proof: If a descending chain x_0 contains x_1 contains ... existed, the set of its members would violate regularity; conversely regularity implies every set has a rank by induction.
consequence: It gives the universe a well-founded structure enabling rank-based induction.

title: Noether's First Theorem on Continuous Symmetries
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Every continuous symmetry of the action of a physical system yields a conserved quantity.
short: Symmetry and conservation laws are two sides of one coin.
detail: Time-translation symmetry gives energy, spatial translation gives momentum, and rotation gives angular momentum.
proof: Invariance of the Lagrangian up to a total derivative implies, via the Euler–Lagrange equations, that a specific combination of momenta and the gauge term is constant along solutions.
consequence: It is the organising principle of modern field theory and explains conservation laws from geometry.

title: The Euler–Lagrange Equations of Variational Calculus
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: A curve that extremises an action integral of the form integral of L(q,q',t) satisfies the Euler–Lagrange equations on its interior.
short: Extremising an integral gives a differential equation for the extremal curve.
detail: The brachistochrone and minimal surface problems are classical applications.
proof: Consider a variation q+epsilon η vanishing at endpoints, differentiate the action with respect to epsilon at zero, integrate the eta-prime term by parts and use the fundamental lemma of the calculus of variations.
consequence: It converts variational principles into the equations of motion of classical mechanics.

title: Hamilton's Canonical Equations of Motion
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: In canonical coordinates (q,p), the dynamics of a Hamiltonian system is governed by q-dot equals the partial derivative of H with respect to p and p-dot equals minus the partial derivative with respect to q.
latex: \dot q=\frac{\partial H}{\partial p},\quad \dot p=-\frac{\partial H}{\partial q}
short: Hamiltonian mechanics trades second-order equations for a symmetric first-order system.
detail: Hamilton's equations preserve the symplectic form on phase space.
proof: Apply the Legendre transform to the Lagrangian and vary the phase-space action; integration by parts gives the two canonical equations.
consequence: It is the bridge from classical to quantum mechanics and to symplectic geometry.

title: The Poisson Bracket as a Lie Algebra Structure
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Poisson bracket of functions f and g on phase space is sum over i of (partial f/partial q_i partial g/partial p_i minus partial f/partial p_i partial g/partial q_i), and it satisfies the Jacobi identity.
latex: \{f,g\}=\sum_i\left(\frac{\partial f}{\partial q_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial p_i}-\frac{\partial f}{\partial p_i}\frac{\partial g}{\partial q_i}\right)
short: Observables form a Lie algebra under the Poisson bracket.
detail: The time derivative of any observable is its Poisson bracket with the Hamiltonian plus an explicit time derivative.
proof: The bracket is bilinear, antisymmetric and satisfies the Jacobi identity by direct differentiation; the evolution formula follows from the chain rule and Hamilton's equations.
consequence: It is the classical counterpart of the quantum commutator.

title: The Legendre Transform and Convex Duality
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Legendre transform of a convex function f is f*(p)=sup over x of (px−f(x)), and for differentiable strictly convex f it is an involution.
short: The Legendre transform swaps a function with the family of its tangent-line intercepts.
detail: It converts a Lagrangian into a Hamiltonian and appears throughout convex optimisation.
proof: If f is convex and differentiable, the supremum occurs where p=f'(x); applying the transform again recovers f by the supporting-line characterisation of convexity.
consequence: It is the mathematical engine behind Hamiltonian mechanics and convex duality.

title: The Principle of Stationary Action
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Physical trajectories make the action functional stationary under small variations with fixed endpoints, rather than necessarily minimal.
short: Nature picks paths where first-order changes of the action vanish.
detail: Stationary includes minima, maxima and saddle points; Fermat's principle of least time is a related variational principle.
proof: For a one-parameter family of paths with fixed endpoints, the first derivative of the action vanishes exactly when the Euler–Lagrange equations hold.
consequence: It unifies mechanics, optics and field theory in a single variational language.

title: The Time-Dependent Schrödinger Equation
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The state of a nonrelativistic quantum system evolves according to iħ times the time derivative of the wavefunction equals the Hamiltonian operator acting on it.
short: Quantum time evolution is generated by the Hamiltonian through a first-order equation.
detail: For a time-independent Hamiltonian the solution is exp(−iHt/ħ) applied to the initial state.
proof: The equation is a postulate of quantum mechanics; when H is time-independent, exponentiation of the self-adjoint operator gives a unitary evolution group by Stone's theorem.
consequence: It predicts interference, tunnelling and the entire spectroscopy of atoms and molecules.

title: The Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: For position and momentum observables, the product of their standard deviations in any state is at least ħ/2.
short: Position and momentum cannot both be sharply localised.
detail: The inequality is a consequence of the noncommutation of the corresponding operators and is not a measurement imperfection.
proof:
Apply the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality to (X−)ψ and (P−

)ψ and use the commutator [X,P]=iħ.
consequence: It sets fundamental limits on precision and explains the zero-point energy of quantum systems.

title: Canonical Quantisation and the Commutation Relations
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Canonical quantisation replaces classical phase-space variables by operators satisfying [q_i,p_j]=iħ δ_ij and replaces Poisson brackets by commutators divided by iħ.
short: Quantum mechanics is obtained by turning classical brackets into operator commutators.
detail: The correspondence is a guiding rule rather than a rigorous functor and has ordering ambiguities for nonlinear expressions.
proof: Dirac's rule identifies the classical Poisson bracket structure with the commutator algebra of observables; the Stone–von Neumann theorem gives uniqueness of the representation for finitely many degrees of freedom.
consequence: It provides the standard route from classical to quantum theories.

title: The Pauli Matrices and Spin-One-half
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The three Pauli matrices are Hermitian 2 by 2 matrices whose pairwise products give i times the remaining matrix; they represent spin-one-half observables and satisfy σ_i σ_j = δ_ij I + i ε_ijk σ_k.
short: A pair of complex matrices encodes the algebra of spin.
detail: They also generate the fundamental representation of SU(2) and square to the identity.
proof: Direct multiplication of the explicit matrices gives the anticommutation and commutation relations.
consequence: They are the building blocks of two-level quantum systems and of the Dirac equation.

title: The Dirac Equation for Relativistic Spinors
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Dirac equation (i γ^μ ∂_μ − m)ψ=0 is a relativistic wave equation whose gamma matrices satisfy the Clifford algebra relations and whose solutions describe spin-one-half particles and antiparticles.
short: Factoring the relativistic energy relation yields a first-order equation with spin built in.
detail: The gamma matrices satisfy {γ^μ,γ^ν}=2η^{μν}I, and squaring the operator recovers the Klein–Gordon equation.
proof: Dirac found matrices whose anticommutators reproduce the Minkowski metric, so applying the conjugate operator gives the relativistic dispersion relation.
consequence: It predicted antimatter and is the foundation of relativistic quantum field theory.

title: Lorentz Transformations and the Invariance of the Speed of Light
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Transformations between inertial frames preserve the spacetime interval c²t²−x²−y²−z² and form the Lorentz group.
short: Different observers disagree about space and time but agree on the spacetime interval.
detail: They lead to time dilation and length contraction and contain rotations as a subgroup.
proof: Requiring the speed of light to be the same in all inertial frames and the transformations to be linear forces preservation of the Minkowski quadratic form.
consequence: It is the geometric foundation of special relativity.

title: The Stress–Energy Tensor and Local Conservation Laws
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The stress–energy tensor encodes the density and flux of energy and momentum, and its divergence vanishes in the absence of external forces.
short: Local conservation of energy and momentum is expressed by a vanishing divergence.
detail: In general relativity the partial derivative becomes a covariant derivative, and the tensor acts as the source of gravity.
proof: Noether's theorem applied to spacetime translations yields four conserved currents, assembled into T^{μν}; their divergence vanishes on the equations of motion.
consequence: It is the universal language for energy transport in field theories.

title: Maxwell's Equations in Differential Form
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Using exterior calculus, Maxwell's equations become dF=0 and d star F = J, where F is the electromagnetic field two-form and J the current three-form.
short: The four Maxwell equations compress into two geometric statements.
detail: The first equation implies the existence locally of a potential one-form A with F=dA.
proof: Writing the electric and magnetic fields as components of F and applying the exterior derivative reproduces the homogeneous Maxwell equations; the codifferential gives the inhomogeneous ones.
consequence: This formulation makes gauge invariance and relativistic covariance transparent.

title: Gauge Invariance and Covariant Derivatives
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Replacing ordinary derivatives by covariant derivatives built from a connection makes field equations invariant under local symmetry transformations.
short: Gauge fields compensate for spacetime-dependent symmetry rotations.
detail: The curvature of the connection is the gauge field strength.
proof: Under a local gauge transformation the connection changes inhomogeneously so that D_μψ transforms covariantly; the commutator of covariant derivatives gives the curvature, which transforms homogeneously.
consequence: It is the common structure underlying electromagnetism, Yang–Mills theory and general relativity.

title: The Aharonov–Bohm Effect
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Charged particles can be affected by an electromagnetic potential in a region where the electric and magnetic fields vanish, through the topology of the configuration space.
short: Even with zero field, a nontrivial potential can shift quantum phases.
detail: It demonstrates that gauge potentials have physical significance beyond the classical fields.
proof: Electrons travelling around a solenoid enclosing magnetic flux acquire a relative phase equal to the enclosed flux in appropriate units, producing a measurable interference shift.
consequence: It reveals the role of topology and holonomy in quantum physics.

title: Yang–Mills Gauge Theory and Field Strength
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: Yang–Mills theory generalises electromagnetism to nonabelian gauge groups, with field strength given by the curvature F=dA+A∧A and equations D star F=0.
short: Noncommuting gauge symmetries produce self-interacting force fields.
detail: The nonabelian term A∧A is what makes the theory nonlinear.
proof: The field strength arises as the commutator of covariant derivatives, and the Yang–Mills equations are the Euler–Lagrange equations of the action integral of tr(F∧star F).
consequence: It describes the strong and weak nuclear interactions.

title: The Gauge Group of the Standard Model
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Standard Model of particle physics is based on the gauge group SU(3) times SU(2) times U(1), describing the strong, weak and electromagnetic interactions.
short: Three symmetry groups organise all known elementary particles and forces except gravity.
detail: Spontaneous symmetry breaking reduces the electroweak part to electromagnetic U(1).
proof: Matter fields are assigned representations of the group; requiring local gauge invariance forces the introduction of gauge bosons transforming under the adjoint representation.
consequence: It is the most thoroughly tested framework in fundamental physics.

title: The Boltzmann Transport Equation
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: The Boltzmann equation describes the evolution of the distribution of particles in phase space under streaming and collisions.
short: It is the kinetic-theory analogue of a conservation law with a collision term.
detail: The collision operator drives the distribution toward local thermodynamic equilibrium.
proof: Balance of particles in a phase-space volume gives the streaming terms; modelling collisions by a bilinear integral operator gives C[f].
consequence: It underlies transport coefficients, hydrodynamic limits and the H-theorem.

title: Entropy and the Second Law of Thermodynamics
subject: Mathematical Physics
statement: In an isolated system, thermodynamic entropy never decreases; in statistical mechanics entropy is proportional to the logarithm of the number of accessible microstates.
short: Disorder grows because there are overwhelmingly more disordered configurations.
detail: Boltzmann's H-theorem gives a mechanical account of entropy increase under molecular chaos assumptions.
